title: Longitudinal Clinical Outcomes After Intra‐Articular Dexamethasone–Lidocaine Injection for Temporomandibular Joint Arthralgia
html:
Among 191 adults with temporomandibular joint arthralgia, intra-articular dexamethasone–lidocaine injection was followed by reductions in pain intensity and pain-location burden and a modest increase in comfortable mouth opening, while maximum mouth opening showed no consistent longitudinal change. Multidomain assessment captured complementary clinical trajectories after injection.


ABSTRACT

Background

Longitudinal real-world data on intra-articular dexamethasone–lidocaine injection for temporomandibular joint (TMJ) arthralgia remain limited. This study evaluated post-injection clinical trajectories in patients with TMJ arthralgia.

Methods

This retrospective observational study included 191 patients (45.5 ± 20.7 years; 67.5% female) with TMJ arthralgia who received intra-articular dexamethasone–lidocaine injection. Mean follow-up from baseline injection to the last available follow-up was 77.0 ± 82.7 days. Outcomes included visual analogue scale (VAS), comfortable mouth opening (CMO), maximum mouth opening (MMO), pain presence, and pain-location burden. Paired, longitudinal, and final-outcome analyses were performed, with additional exploratory analyses.

Results

At first follow-up, VAS decreased from 3.25 ± 1.75 to 2.45 ± 1.67 (change, −0.80 ± 1.44; FDR-adjusted p < 0.001), CMO increased modestly by 0.99 ± 5.98 mm (FDR-adjusted p = 0.015), and pain-location burden decreased by 0.30 ± 0.90 (FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). MMO did not change significantly (FDR-adjusted p = 0.166). Mixed-effects models using actual elapsed time showed decreases in VAS (β = −0.069 per 30 days; FDR-adjusted p = 0.003) and pain-location burden (β = −0.093 per 30 days; FDR-adjusted p < 0.001) and a modest increase in CMO (β = 0.343 mm per 30 days; FDR-adjusted p = 0.001), whereas MMO showed no significant longitudinal change. The absolute VAS decrease was greater in the moderate-to-severe baseline pain group than in the mild pain group (−1.68 ± 1.56 vs. −0.35 ± 1.13; FDR-adjusted p < 0.001). At final follow-up, VAS had decreased from baseline in 53.4% of patients, including 80.0% of those with moderate-to-severe baseline pain (FDR-adjusted p < 0.001).

Conclusions

Intra-articular dexamethasone–lidocaine injection was followed by decreases in pain intensity and pain-location burden and a modest increase in CMO, whereas MMO showed no consistent longitudinal change. These findings support a multidomain approach to assessing clinical trajectories after TMJ injection.
